mcqs.question: The narration loop is: state approach, state complexity, then code. Why say the complexity before writing anything?
options: It gives the interviewer a concrete claim to verify against the code you're about to write
It's required by most interview rubrics as a checklist item
It commits you to a plan you can't change later
It replaces the need to test the code afterward
mcqs.explanation: Stating the complexity up front gives the interviewer a specific, checkable claim to compare against what you actually type, which is what makes the narration useful rather than decorative. It's not a rigid commitment — a stated approach can and should change if you spot a problem, and it says nothing about skipping testing.

mcqs.question: A candidate goes silent for four minutes while working out a solution, then delivers a correct answer. Why does this typically score worse than narrating the same thinking aloud?
options: Silence is against most interview rules and gets penalized automatically
It always means the candidate is guessing rather than reasoning
It signals the candidate doesn't know the answer's complexity
The interviewer can't distinguish productive thinking from being stalled, and loses visibility into any partial progress
mcqs.explanation: From outside, silent deep thought and silent stalling look identical, and the interviewer also loses any chance to credit partial progress made along the way. It isn't a formal rule violation, doesn't necessarily mean guessing, and says nothing about whether complexity was considered.

mcqs.question: A candidate narrates every line - declaring each variable, each loop bound - in full sentences. What's the actual problem with this style?
options: It takes too many words to be grammatically correct
The one sentence that carries real reasoning gets buried under sentences that carry none
It's technically inaccurate about what the code does
Interviewers prefer candidates who type in complete silence
mcqs.explanation: The cost isn't length for its own sake — it's that decisions (why this data structure, why this order) become indistinguishable from mechanical transcription of the code, so the interviewer has to dig for the signal. It's not about grammar, accuracy, or a preference for silence.

mcqs.question: A candidate jumps straight to an optimal O(n) solution with no mention of a brute force. The code is correct. What's missing from the interviewer's perspective?
options: Nothing - correctness at the best complexity is the entire signal
A demonstration that the candidate can write comments
Proof that the candidate recognized the naive approach and consciously improved on it, versus pattern-matching to the answer
Evidence that the candidate can code in more than one language
mcqs.explanation: Naming the brute force first is what lets the interviewer see the reasoning behind the optimization, not just its result — without it, a memorized-optimal solution and a genuinely-derived one look the same. Correctness alone doesn't establish that distinction, and the other options aren't what this practice demonstrates.

mcqs.question: Why is proactively saying "this is O(n squared); I can get it to O(n log n) with a sort" stronger than waiting for the interviewer to ask if it can be faster?
options: It shows self-critical evaluation of your own work and hands the interviewer a natural decision point, rather than making them find the gap
It guarantees a higher score regardless of whether you implement the faster version
It shortens the total interview time
It is required whenever a solution isn't O(1)
mcqs.explanation: Volunteering the trade-off demonstrates you can critique your own solution unprompted, and gives the interviewer an easy branch — dig deeper or move on — instead of spending their own time spotting the limitation. It doesn't guarantee a score, isn't primarily about saving time, and isn't a universal requirement for every complexity class.
